reviewer_discipline.rule: Read the caller before you judge the callee.
Judge the change against its contract, not against your preferred style.
One finding, one cause. If a sentence needs "and" twice, split it.
Name the defect class. "This is fragile" is not a finding. "This crashes when Finish is blank" is.
Prefer the smallest fix that removes the defect. Do not attach a rewrite to a bug fix.
Say when a finding is pre-existing. Do not blame the current change for old debt.
If the code is good, say so in one line and stop. Do not manufacture findings.

checks.check: Does each branch match the stated contract?
Are units, scales, and rounding consistent across the flow?
Is the same value computed twice in two places? If yes, one will drift.
Do the tests assert the contract, or only the current output?
Is any default value silently accepted where an error is safer?
Empty collection, single item, and duplicates.
Null, missing, or whitespace-only input at every public entry point.
Zero, negative, and very large numbers. Also boundary values: first, last, exactly the limit.
Order independence: does the result change if items arrive in a different order?
Repeat calls: is the operation safe to run twice?
Concurrent or re-entrant calls, if the code can be reached that way.
Partial failure: half the items succeed, then the rest fail.
Is every failure visible to the caller or the log, or is it swallowed?
Is a catch block doing real work, or hiding a defect?
Does a failure leave the system in a half-changed state?
Does the error message name the input and the expected range?
Is a retry safe, bounded, and free of fixed delays?
Does cleanup run on every exit path, including the error path?
Does each name say what the value means, not how it is stored?
Can a reader follow one screen without scrolling back?
Is nesting deeper than three levels? If yes, ask for guard clauses.
Are boolean parameters explained by name at the call site, or are they a trap?
Does a comment explain why, rather than repeat what the line says?
Would a new team member need to ask a question to change this safely?
Does each unit have one reason to change?
Does a low-level unit know about a high-level concern: UI, file system, clock, network?
Is a dependency created inside the unit instead of passed in?
Is a rule stated in two places? The second copy will rot.
Are the boundaries of the project respected: no UI or platform calls from the core logic?
Is a public method wider than it needs to be?
Is work repeated inside a loop that could be done once before it?
Is a collection enumerated more than once when once would do?
Is memory or a handle owned, and released on every path?
Is a cache correct, or does it serve stale data after a change?
Is the hot path doing logging, formatting, or allocation it does not need?
Is a measurement claimed without a measurement? Ask for numbers or drop the claim.
Is external input validated before use, not after the damage?
Are secrets, tokens, personal data, or file contents written to logs or reports?
Is a path joined from user input without normalisation?
Is a permission, a guard, or an authorisation check missing on a new entry point?
Is a dependency added for a task the platform already does?
Is deserialisation or reflection used on untrusted input?
Does each new failure branch have a test that makes it fire?
Do the tests fail if you revert the fix? If not, they prove nothing.
Do the test names state the behaviour, not the method name?
Is a risky path tested only through the happy path?
Are time, culture, ordering, and randomness controlled in the test?
Was a test deleted, weakened, or skipped to make the build pass?
Is the concept documented once, in the place a reader will look first?
Is the new code consistent with its neighbours, or a second style?
Is configuration kept out of the logic?
Will a change to this behaviour require edits in many files?
Is there an escape hatch for the next case, or has the design hard-coded today's case?

contract_first_checks.note: These apply when the repository states them. Read the contract and use its words, not yours.
contract_first_checks.check: Stated architectural invariants are treated as blockers when broken.
A validation branch that rejects bad input ships with a test that feeds it bad input.
Deterministic identifiers, ordering, culture, time, and rounding are preserved.
No fixed sleeps for synchronisation. Poll a named condition with a deadline.
No exceptions swallowed to keep the build green.
No test deleted, skipped, or loosened to reach green.
No new dependency without a stated reason and a check that the platform cannot already do it.
No duplicated rule: one source of truth per policy.

noise_control.rule: Never report what a formatter, linter, or analyser already enforces. It wastes the reader's attention.
Never report pure taste: brace style, comment wording, method order, or naming you simply prefer.
Never report an issue you cannot tie to a broken input, a wrong outcome, or a recurring cost.
Never repeat the same finding for each call site. Report it once and list the sites.
Never pad the report to look thorough. A short, sharp report gets acted on.
Report a pre-existing defect once, labelled as pre-existing, and only when it touches this change.

proof_rules.rule: A defect claim needs a concrete input and the wrong result it produces.
A cost claim needs a number, a frequency, or a named scenario. Otherwise it is a guess.
A behaviour-preserving claim needs a named test that runs before and after the change.
A performance claim needs a measurement you took, or it is dropped.
An API claim needs a signature you read: source, installed metadata, or official documentation.
When you cannot check, write "unknown" and say what would settle it.
